theme: Baal of Peor; Phinehas; the second census; Joshua commissioned
readingInstruction: Read Numbers 25:1-27:23. This reading includes a terrible sin at Baal of Peor, the zeal of Phinehas, a new census, the daughters of Zelophehad, and the commissioning of Joshua. Notice the way the story turns from failure to a new beginning.
settingTheScene: Israel is still on the plains of Moab. After Balaam’s oracles, you might expect everything to be well, but chapter 25 tells how the people joined in the worship of Baal of Peor and with Moabite women. A plague breaks out. Chapter 26 then begins a new census of the next generation, which is a way of marking that the old generation has gone. Chapter 27 deals with the inheritance rights of women and the appointment of Moses’ successor.
observation: “While Israel lived in Shittim, the people began to whore with the daughters of Moab” (25:1).
They join in the worship of Baal of Peor, and the LORD’s anger is kindled (25:2-3).
Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, takes a spear and kills an Israelite man and a Midianite woman (25:6-8).
The plague stops, with 24,000 dead, and God makes a covenant of peace with Phinehas and his descendants (25:9-13).
A new census is taken, and “among these there was not one of those listed by Moses and Aaron… except Caleb… and Joshua” (26:64-65).
The five daughters of Zelophehad ask for their father’s inheritance, since he had no sons (27:1-4).
God says, “The daughters of Zelophehad are right” and makes a law for the inheritance of daughters (27:5-11).
Moses asks God to appoint a leader, and God says, “Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit” (27:15-23).
interpretation:
The sin of Baal of Peor shows how Israel’s most dangerous enemy is not the army of a neighboring king but the attraction of other gods. Balaam, who could not curse Israel, found another way: he advised Balak to send women to seduce the Israelite men into idolatry (31:16). What a hired curse could not do, temptation did. The people fall into sexual immorality and the worship of a false god, the two sins that regularly appear together in the Bible. The plague that follows shows the seriousness of the offense.

Phinehas’ action is hard to read. His zeal for God’s honor stops the plague, and God commends him. But it is a violent act, in a setting where the nation was under the covenant penalties of the theocracy. It is not a model for private revenge. It shows the principle that when the community is polluted by sin, someone must stand in the gap. The promise of a “covenant of peace” to Phinehas is a reminder that even in judgment, God works through faithful servants.

The new census marks the end of the old generation. “Not one” was left except Caleb and Joshua. It is a quiet but powerful way of confirming God’s word: what he said at Kadesh has come true. The people who feared the giants are gone, and their children are numbered. God keeps his word, both in judgment and in promise.

The story of the daughters of Zelophehad is a bright spot. The five sisters speak up in faith, believing that the land will be given and wanting a share in it. They come forward at a time when the old generation has just been shown to have lost its vision. Moses brings their case to God, and God says, “They are right.” The inheritance laws are changed to include them. It is a case of faith being rewarded and the justice of God extending to those who might be overlooked.

The chapter ends with the commissioning of Joshua. Moses will not lead Israel into the land, and so a successor is appointed. He is a man “in whom is the Spirit,” and he is publicly ordained with the laying on of hands.
connection: Paul warns the Corinthians about the sin at Peor (1 Corinthians 10:8). Revelation 2:14 refers to the teaching of Balaam. Psalm 106:30-31 says that Phinehas’ action was “counted to him as righteousness.” Jesus, whose name is the Greek form of Joshua’s, is the greater leader who brings his people into the true rest (Hebrews 4:8-9). The daughters of Zelophehad point forward to the truth that in Christ, there is “neither male nor female” in the inheritance (Galatians 3:28-29).
application:
Think about where you are most vulnerable to temptation, and take a concrete step to guard it.

Take heart from the daughters of Zelophehad. Ask God for something in faith, believing that he will keep his promises.

Pray for the next generation of leaders in your church, that they would be filled with the Spirit.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to guard your heart against rival loves.
Thank him for keeping his word across generations.
Pray for leaders filled with his Spirit.
